content.question_text: How is the ambiguity solved when the same method is defined as default in an interface and also as a concrete method in a superclass?

core_requirements: The superclass method wins.
acceptable_variations: Superclass wins.
Class method overrides interface default.

content.question_text: How is the problem solved when two interfaces provide a default method with exactly the same name and parameter types?

core_requirements: You must override the method — otherwise the compiler reports an error.
acceptable_variations: You must override it.
Compile-time error if not overridden.

content.question_text: What happens if two interfaces have a method with the same name and parameter types, but only one is default?

core_requirements: The compiler still reports an error — if either interface contains an implementation, there is a conflict.
acceptable_variations: Compiler error.
Conflict exists if one is default.

content.question_text: What happens if neither of the shared methods in two interfaces are default?

core_requirements: No conflict — the implementing class must implement the method.
acceptable_variations: No conflict.
Implementing class must provide implementation.

content.question_text: What is a callback pattern in programming?

core_requirements: A pattern that allows you to specify the action that should occur whenever a particular event happens.
acceptable_variations: Passing a behavior to be executed later.
A function or object that is called back when something happens.

content.question_text: What is the object-oriented approach to implementing callbacks in Java?

core_requirements: You pass an object of a class that implements a specific interface.
The framework/component then calls a method on that object when the event occurs.
acceptable_variations: Pass an object that implements a callback interface.
The callback is an object with a known method that gets invoked.

content.question_text: Why is passing an object more flexible than passing a bare function for callbacks in Java?

core_requirements: An object can carry additional information (state) beyond just the method to be called.
This allows for more complex and stateful callbacks.
acceptable_variations: Objects can hold state and data.
More flexible because you can store additional information in the object.

content.question_text: In the callback pattern, what is the role of the interface (e.g., ActionListener)?

core_requirements: It defines the contract that the callback object must fulfill.
It specifies which method the framework will call.
acceptable_variations: It acts as a contract between the caller and the callback.
It defines the method signature the callback must implement.

content.question_text: How does a framework (like Timer) know which method to call on a callback object?

core_requirements: The framework uses the interface that the callback object implements.
It calls the specific method defined by that interface.
acceptable_variations: Through the interface contract.
Because the object implements a known interface with a known method.

content.question_text: What is the purpose of the Comparator interface when there is already a compareTo method?

core_requirements: It is used to compare objects in a different way than the compareTo method.
It allows custom ordering without modifying the class itself.
acceptable_variations: To define alternative sorting orders.
For custom comparison logic outside the class.

content.question_text: How do you use the Comparator interface?

core_requirements: Create a class that implements Comparator and implement the compare method with your custom logic (or supply a lambda for the same purpose).
acceptable_variations: Implement Comparator and override compare()
Use a lambda to define the comparison.

content.question_text: How do you actually use a class/lambda that implements Comparator?

core_requirements: Use it as an argument in a sorting method, e.g. Arrays.sort(arr, comparatorInstance) or list.sort(comparatorInstance).
acceptable_variations: Pass it to Arrays.sort() or Collections.sort().
As a comparator argument in sorting methods.

content.question_text: What is the name of the built-in case-insensitive comparator for String?

core_requirements: String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER
acceptable_variations: CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER

content.question_text: Why can't you shuffle an array by sorting it with a random comparator?

core_requirements: The sorting algorithm may detect that the comparator violates its contract (e.g., not transitive), since results differ between calls.
It could throw an exception.
acceptable_variations: Random comparators violate the Comparator contract.
Sorting expects a consistent order — random breaks it.

content.question_text: How do you properly shuffle an array in Java?

core_requirements: Convert to a List and use Collections.shuffle().
acceptable_variations: Use Collections.shuffle() on a List.
Convert array to list, shuffle, then convert back.

content.question_text: What are the three rules a Comparator must fulfill?

core_requirements: Reflexivity — comparing an element to itself (or an equal element) returns 0.
Antisymmetry — swapping the arguments swaps the sign of the result.
Transitivity — if x comes before y and y comes before z, then x must come before z.
acceptable_variations: Reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive.
Consistent with equals, symmetric, transitive.
